Contributing to opal

Thank you for your interest in contributing to opal. This guide describes how to propose changes, set up a development environment, and the checks a pull request must pass. Contributions of all sizes are welcome, including bug reports, documentation fixes, tests, and new model features.

opal is under active development and interfaces may change. If you are unsure whether a change fits the project, open an issue first.

Where to contribute

Contribution Location
Package code, tests, vignettes, and function documentation N-DucharmeBarth-NOAA/opal
Project website, WCPFC documents, and case-study write-ups N-DucharmeBarth-NOAA/opal-documentation (published at https://connect.fisheries.noaa.gov/opal/)
Bug reports, feature requests, and design discussion opal issues

Issues

Before opening an issue, search existing issues to avoid duplicates.

A bug report should include a minimal reproducible example, the output of sessionInfo(), and the opal version or commit. For numerical problems, state what you expected, what you observed, and how you checked it (for example, against an SS3 or MULTIFAN-CL reference model).

A feature request or substantial change should be discussed in an issue before work starts. Issues intended for implementation, including those assigned to coding agents, should be self-contained, with:

  • the files and functions affected, including exact function signatures;
  • acceptance criteria;
  • whether the change is expected to alter model numerics (see Numerical changes);
  • backward-compatibility implications and expected effects on existing tests;
  • notes on AD safety for any code that operates on estimated quantities.

Branches and pull requests

  • main is the stable release branch.
  • dev is the active development branch.

Create a feature branch from dev and open pull requests against dev. Keep each pull request focused on one change. A pull request should:

  1. describe what changed and why, and link the relevant issue;
  2. state whether model numerics change, and if so follow the regeneration protocol below;
  3. add or update tests for new or changed behaviour;
  4. update roxygen documentation and vignettes when exported function signatures or behaviour change;
  5. add a NEWS.md entry for user-visible or numerical changes.

Development environments

Open a GitHub Codespace from Code → Codespaces to build the development environment automatically. CI, Codespaces, and the Copilot coding agent use renv.lock as the single source of truth for the R version and package records.

All environments run .github/scripts/setup-r-env.R, which restores the packages and applies the TMB OSA-header and compResidual installation workarounds. To restore locally, first install the R version recorded in renv.lock and the required system libraries, then run from the repository root:

Rscript .github/scripts/setup-r-env.R

In Codespaces, locked GitHub packages are downloaded from public commit archives first, avoiding API rate limits and repository-scoped token restrictions. If that fails, setup tries the original API URL. Package versions and commit SHAs still come from renv.lock; do not install newer GitHub versions to work around a download failure.

The Ubuntu policy and Quarto CLI version default are documented in .github/actions/setup-opal-env/action.yml; Codespaces must match them. Workflow-specific tools not recorded in the lockfile remain explicit installs after the shared setup.

After intentional dependency updates, run renv::snapshot() and commit renv.lock. Commit R-version updates in that lockfile too; CI, Codespaces, and Copilot follow it without separate version edits.

Copilot reads its thin setup-workflow wrapper from the default branch, main, but uses the working checkout’s environment definition. Scheduled runs and manual runs on main with ref: dev warm caches for dev-based tasks. After merging environment setup changes to main, maintainers should run that manual setup, merge main into dev, and check that a dev-based Copilot task restores the cache.

Development workflow

  • Load the package with devtools::load_all() rather than source().
  • After editing roxygen comments, run devtools::document(). The document.yaml workflow also regenerates man/ and NAMESPACE on pushes that touch R/, and commits the result, so pull before continuing work on a branch.
  • Run devtools::test() before opening a pull request. Run devtools::check() for changes that affect exports, dependencies, or documentation.
  • Prefer small, targeted changes. Refactors that touch several files or array dimensions should be proposed in an issue first, with their effect on test fixtures described.

Code guidelines

AD safety

Model code runs on RTMB’s automatic-differentiation tape. Any function that may receive AD values must:

  • declare the relevant overloads at the top of the function, for example "[<-" <- ADoverload("[<-") (and "c" <- ADoverload("c") where needed);
  • avoid base R coercions that strip the advector class, such as matrix() or as.vector() on AD values. Fix type loss where it occurs, not in the receiving function;
  • take derived biological quantities (for example M_a, spawning_potential_a, weight_fya) as explicit arguments rather than reading them from data, so gradients propagate when the underlying parameters are estimated.

After a change, confirm that obj$fn(obj$par) and obj$gr(obj$par) return finite values.

Exported functions

Exported functions are documented in man/ and used in vignettes and tests. Changing a signature requires updating the roxygen documentation, NAMESPACE, affected vignettes, and tests in the same pull request.

Model components

  • Selectivity: changes to selectivity forms must update the par_sel dimensions, get_map(), and get_bounds() together.
  • Composition likelihoods: data flow from raw data through prep_lf_data() or prep_wf_data() to flattened vectors and then to get_length_like() or get_weight_like(). lf_switch and wf_switch select the likelihood. Changes to one stage must be checked against the others.
  • Observations: mark observed data with OBS() so that obj$simulate() and one-step-ahead residuals remain available.

Documentation style

Documentation and vignettes should be factual and concise. Avoid promotional language. State limitations and known differences from other platforms directly.

Tests

Tests use testthat edition 3.

  • Shared fixtures are in tests/testthat/helper-*.R (for example opaka_inputs(), opaka_obj(), and synth_*() helpers). Do not build models at the top level of test files; use the cached helpers.

  • Numerical reference outputs are in tests/testthat/_reference/. Never create or overwrite reference files from within a test.

  • Simulation self-tests are skipped by default. Run them locally with:

    Sys.setenv(OPAL_SELFTEST = "true", OPAL_SELFTEST_NSIM = "30")
devtools::test(filter = "selftest")

    OPAL_SELFTEST_START may be "truth" (default) or "default", and OPAL_SELFTEST_OUT saves results to a directory. Self-tests also run in .github/workflows/selftest.yaml. Calibration limits are documented at the top of each self-test file; do not change them without rerunning the calibration and recording it there.

Performance benchmarks

.github/workflows/benchmark.yaml runs independently of the numerical and simulation tests. Its memory job runs on every pull request to dev or main, weekly against dev, and on manual dispatch. The PR timing-ab job installs the exact PR BASE and HEAD in separate libraries outside the checkouts and measures them interleaved on the same runner. PR timing uses five paired rounds of four indicative cases: objectives and gradients for Opakapaka and IO YFT. BET timing, tape construction, reports, repeated fits, trajectories and Hessians remain in the full weekly suite and the unchanged memory suite. In hosted validation the PR timing measurement step took 7–11 minutes, within its 20-minute PR timeout; setup and uncached dependency restoration add to the job time. Each measured case/round still runs in a fresh subprocess. A/B reuses one separate, fresh idle reference per installed library across the job, rather than reloading the same idle package before every round; this matches how the multi-case memory runner subtracts one idle reference.

PR timing measures GitHub’s test merge commit against its first parent, the target-branch tip it merged, so target-branch changes are not attributed to the PR. Rounds alternate whether BASE or HEAD runs first.

Optimizer-path metrics, meaning fit counts (fn_evals, gr_evals, iterations) and the fit cases’ mem_alloc_bytes, are compared BASE versus HEAD within timing-ab, one fit per revision on the same runner, not against the committed baseline. They are deterministic on one machine but differ between hosted CPU models: identical code gave 1225 BET fn evaluations on an AMD EPYC 9V45 and 1651 on an Intel Xeon 8370C, and allocated 30% more on the latter. PRs gate the well-conditioned opaka_fit (+10% fails; performance-accepted does not waive count failures). The full profile also compares bet_fit and io_yft_fit_evals, but only warns, because their paths change with harmless floating-point rounding. The committed baseline records these metrics as trends; it still gates the fit cases’ peak RSS and structural size, which do not depend on the path.

Weekly timing-ab retains the full 17-case, ten-round suite, comparing two separately installed copies of the same exact dev SHA. This checks same-runner stability, not cumulative timing creep; daily instruction counts provide the committed-baseline creep gate. Manual dispatch also compares BASE=HEAD at the dispatched revision; select timing_profile: smoke for the PR profile or full (default) for the weekly profile. For BASE-versus-HEAD coverage of BET, tape construction, trajectories, reports, Hessians and the BET/IO YFT fit counts, dispatch on the PR branch with base_ref set to the target branch or SHA and timing_profile: full; this on-demand comparison is not a required PR check. Each scheduled or manual run has its own concurrency group, so queued calibration runs are never cancelled; superseded PR runs are.

The full memory suite runs on PRs and records every workload against the committed baseline. The instructions job uses Valgrind on daily and manual runs only. OPAL_BENCHMARK_FULL_FITS controls only the costly io_yft_fit_evals case: it is enabled on scheduled and manual runs and disabled on PRs. All jobs use the shared Ubuntu 22.04 environment and one OpenMP, OpenBLAS, and MKL thread.

Benchmarks are opt-in locally. From the repository root, install the package into a separate library, then run memory measurements:

mkdir -p benchmark-out/head-lib
R CMD INSTALL --library="$PWD/benchmark-out/head-lib" .
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 MKL_NUM_THREADS=1
export OPAL_BENCHMARK=true OPAL_BENCHMARK_ROOT="$PWD"
export OPAL_BENCHMARK_OUT="$PWD/benchmark-out"
export OPAL_BENCHMARK_LIBRARY="$PWD/benchmark-out/head-lib"
export OPAL_BENCHMARK_TOL=0.10
OPAL_BENCHMARK_LAYER=memory Rscript -e \
  'testthat::test_local(filter = "benchmark-models", stop_on_failure = TRUE)'

For instruction counts, install Valgrind and run OPAL_BENCHMARK_LAYER=instructions Rscript dev/run-benchmark-instructions.R with the same environment. To reproduce PR timing, install BASE and HEAD in separate libraries, set OPAL_BENCHMARK_BASE_LIBRARY and OPAL_BENCHMARK_HEAD_LIBRARY to their absolute paths, and run OPAL_BENCHMARK_TIMING_PROFILE=smoke OPAL_BENCHMARK_ROUNDS=5 Rscript dev/run-benchmark-ab.R. For the full suite use OPAL_BENCHMARK_TIMING_PROFILE=full and OPAL_BENCHMARK_ROUNDS=10. Both retain the 10% threshold and fail timing only when the lower 95% ratio confidence bound exceeds 1.10. Do not reuse a loaded package between revisions. Workflow artifacts retain measurements and environment metadata; the job summaries report results even when a regression fails. Re-running a workflow deletes the previous attempt’s artifacts (its job summary remains), so download them before re-running.

The default regression tolerance is 0.10 (10%). Manual dispatch accepts a tolerance fraction and an update_baseline boolean. Set update_baseline to generate candidate baselines, or set OPAL_BENCHMARK_UPDATE=true locally. Download the artifacts, review the measured changes and metadata, and explicitly merge the memory artifact’s baseline.rds and instruction artifact’s instructions.rds before committing. The committed tests/testthat/_benchmark/baseline.rds stores all layers together in its results table; instructions.rds is an intermediate artifact, not a second tracked baseline. The workflow never commits or pushes. Baselines are measurements, not universal constants: refresh them on the documented Ubuntu environment after changes to the runner image, R, dependencies, or benchmark definitions. Do not treat measurements from another machine as calibrated hosted baselines.

With the same environment as above, explicit regeneration commands are:

# Regenerate measured baselines (20 timing samples for applicable cases).
OPAL_BENCHMARK_FULL_FITS=true Rscript dev/update-benchmark-baseline.R 20
# Regenerate deterministic replay trajectories after reviewing model changes.
Rscript dev/update-benchmark-trajectories.R opaka bet io_yft
# Produce reviewable instruction measurements without gating against old values.
OPAL_BENCHMARK_UPDATE=true OPAL_BENCHMARK_LAYER=instructions \
  Rscript dev/run-benchmark-instructions.R
# Regenerate memory/timing baselines and merge reviewed instruction measurements.
OPAL_BENCHMARK_FULL_FITS=true \
  Rscript dev/update-benchmark-baseline.R 20 benchmark-out/instructions.rds

For a dispatched update, extract the reviewed benchmark-memory and benchmark-instructions artifacts, then explicitly combine them, recording the reviewed run/attempt/artifact URLs:

Rscript dev/combine-benchmark-baseline.R \
  benchmark-out/memory/baseline.rds benchmark-out/instructions/instructions.rds \
  --hosted https://github.com/N-DucharmeBarth-NOAA/opal/actions/runs/<run>/attempts/<n> \
  https://github.com/N-DucharmeBarth-NOAA/opal/actions/runs/<run>/artifacts/<id>

The script requires all four instruction cases and every memory, timing and fit-count metric. A partial artifact cannot replace layer-wide provenance.

For an intentional A/B time or memory regression, explain the trade-off in a nonempty Performance rationale: ... line in the PR description. A repository maintainer with maintain or admin permission may apply performance-accepted. Label additions/removals and PR description edits retrigger the workflow, so removing acceptance re-enables the gate. Before checking out PR code, the workflow checks the live PR label, rationale, latest label actor, and that actor’s current repository permission through the read-only GitHub API. Missing evidence or API failure keeps the gate enabled. This exception covers the same-runner A/B comparison only; it does not suppress measurements or waive the committed-baseline memory gate, fit-count regressions, or instruction regressions. Fork PRs use pull_request, not pull_request_target, and receive no elevated token.

Hosted calibration and validation (2026-11-04)

Validation ran on the PR branch through a temporary push trigger, since workflow_dispatch needs the workflow on the default branch. Each pushed commit selected jobs and settings in its message. A temporary, opt-in injection mechanism provided the regressions. The trigger and the injection code were removed afterwards (498ef62 and the following commit). All runs used Ubuntu 22.04, R 4.5.2 and one OMP/OpenBLAS/MKL thread. Hosted runners varied between Intel Xeon 8370C/8573C and AMD EPYC 7763/9V45/9V74.

In B2, mem_alloc_bytes and structural_bytes failed for all four injected cases. Peak RSS failed for opaka_fn (2.12×), opaka_gr (2.13×) and io_yft_gr (+42 MB, 1.115×). For io_yft_fn it rose 32 MB (1.086×) and passed. The rise exceeded the 5 MiB floor but not 10% of the 368 MB baseline.

Unit tests (test-performance-gates.R, test-benchmark-models.R) cover the comparison logic: the 10% threshold, the 5 MiB RSS floor, same-runner fit counts, paired-bootstrap intervals, baseline merging and A/B provenance. The hosted runs above show the same gates working end to end on GitHub runners.

Known limitations

  • PR timing sensitivity. Timing fails only when the lower interval bound exceeds 1.10. Five rounds reliably catch about 15% on the Opakapaka cases, but on the noisier IO YFT cases only slowdowns of roughly 20–25% or more. Doubling the rounds would narrow intervals by about 30%: still short of reliable 15% detection for IO YFT, and over the 20-minute PR step limit. Smaller slowdowns are caught by the instruction counts, which run daily (below).
  • Peak RSS on large models. Peak RSS must exceed both 5 MiB and 10%, so on the 368 MB IO YFT cases it misses increases below about 37 MB. Allocation and structural size still gate those cases.
  • Runner hardware varies. Fit counts and fit allocations depend on the CPU, so they are compared BASE versus HEAD on one runner, never against the committed baseline. Committed timing rows are reference values, not gates.
  • The harness is part of the PR. timing-ab runs the benchmark harness from the HEAD checkout, so a PR can change its own gate. Review changes to tests/testthat/helper-benchmark.R, helper-performance.R and dev/run-benchmark-*.R as changes to the gate.
  • Untested dispatch path. workflow_dispatch, including base_ref, cannot run until the workflow reaches the default branch. The same jobs ran through the temporary push trigger, but the dispatch inputs themselves are not hosted-tested.

Required checks (maintainer handoff)

Branch protection is configured in repository settings, not by this workflow.

  • Require memory and timing-ab on dev and main.
  • Do not require instructions. It is skipped on PRs, and a skipped status is not evidence of a measurement. It runs daily against dev (all jobs run on Mondays; the other days run only instructions). For a PR expected to affect speed, a maintainer can dispatch the workflow on the PR branch to get instruction counts before merging.
  • performance-accepted waives only A/B timing and memory failures. It never waives fit-count or instruction regressions; those need a reviewed baseline refresh or a fix.
  • When a daily instruction run fails, the regression is already on dev. Bisect the merges since the last passing run.

Numerical changes

The golden test (tests/testthat/test-golden-opaka.R) compares the objective, gradient, and every REPORT() element of the ’opakapaka quickstart model against a stored reference, at both the starting values and the MLE. It also checks that the reference file was produced under the current .opal_model_scientific_version, and that the bundled example fit is compatible with the current model. read_opal_fit() uses the scientific version to identify fits created under an earlier model contract.

A numerical change is any change that alters the objective, gradient, or reported quantities for an existing model configuration. Examples include changes to dynamics, likelihoods, priors, data preparation, parameter transformations, or default values.

Any change that alters model numerics follows the regeneration protocol:

  1. Show the golden test failing.
  2. Document the change in NEWS.md.
  3. Bump .opal_model_scientific_version.
  4. Regenerate tests/testthat/_reference/opaka-quickstart.rds with data-raw/make-test-references.R.
  5. Regenerate inst/extdata/opaka_quickstart_fit.rds with data-raw/generate-opaka-quickstart-fit.R.

All five steps belong in the same pull request. The pull request description should include the golden test failure from step 1 and explain why the new values are correct, for example through comparison with a reference model, an analytical result, or a targeted test of the changed component.

Additional rules:

  • Do not resolve a golden test failure by loosening tolerances.
  • If a change is not intended to alter numerics and the golden test fails, treat the failure as a bug.
  • Adding a new REPORT() element does not require regeneration. Removing or renaming one does, because the golden test checks that all reference elements are still reported.
  • For changes that could affect estimation performance, run the simulation self-tests and report the results in the pull request.

NEWS.md

Add entries under the development version heading at the top of NEWS.md, following the existing format: the date, a link to the commit, and a short description of the change and its consequences. For numerical changes, state that previously saved fits use the earlier scientific model contract.

Vignettes

  • Package vignettes in vignettes/ are built by pkgdown and should run quickly. Expensive computations, such as MCMC, should use pre-computed results cached in inst/extdata/, or be guarded with !identical(Sys.getenv("CI"), "true").
  • Longer development workflows, such as the WCPO bigeye tuna case study and the regression baseline, are in dev/vignettes/ and are not built with the package.

Continuous integration

GitHub Actions run R CMD check on Ubuntu (vignettes are not built during the check), regenerate documentation, run simulation self-tests, and build the pkgdown site. The release pkgdown site is deployed from main; pushes to dev build and deploy development documentation under /opal/dev/. Both builds check local links and retain the rendered site as a workflow artifact. Development vignettes under dev/vignettes/ are run deliberately, separately from the three package vignettes.

Coding agents

Repository conventions for coding agents are in .github/copilot-instructions.md, and apply to any agent used on the repository. When assigning an issue to GitHub Copilot, select dev as the base branch (the default is main). Agent-authored pull requests are reviewed to the same standard as any other, including the numerical-change protocol.
